A1.justification: Both PDFs describe TOPLOC and contain readable text, algorithms, figures, tables and appendices. The retained material can be matched despite substantial reformatting, table consolidation and the addition of Appendix C.

before.justification: v1 reports original UltraChat experiments measuring activation errors, hardware and attention-kernel robustness, and detection of model, prompt and precision changes.

after.justification: v2 retains original inference-verification results and adds, among other evidence, a synthetic modulus-search experiment using 100 million random integer sets in Table 11.

M1.justification: Top-k selection, injective index mapping, polynomial encoding and exponent/mantissa validation retain the same procedure. Appendix C documents implementations of existing subroutines; it does not establish a changed algorithm. The revised experimental thresholds are assessed under E3.

E1.justification: UltraChat, the prompt alterations and the inference-verification scenarios remain. Appendix C adds a narrow synthetic evaluation population: uniformly random sets of 128 int32 integers used to investigate modulus search. The additional Llama-2-13B comparison changes model configuration rather than language-task coverage.

E2.justification: New Section 5.8 and Table 6 introduce a substantive quantitative comparison against zkLLM, SVIP and raw-activation storage across resource costs and detection errors. v1 discussed zkLLM and SVIP in related work and compared raw storage requirements, but lacked this comparative evaluation. Common-setting reruns of all comparators are not documented.

E3.justification: Section 5.2 changes the reported exponent-mismatch thresholds from 90 to 38 for bf16 and from 120 to 8 for fp32, retaining the mantissa thresholds. New evaluations specify Llama-2-13B resource/error metrics and 100 million random 128-integer sets for modulus search. These reported changes do not establish that retained experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: Appendix C/Table 11 adds an analysis of how quickly injective-modulus search succeeds. Conversely, v1 Figure 3's cross-model exponent-error sweep and the maximum-statistic panels in Figure 4 are removed. The remaining top-k, token-index and hardware/kernel stability analyses are largely retained.

E5.justification: Both versions use descriptive extrema, means, medians and observed frequencies without reporting repeated-run uncertainty, seeds, confidence intervals or significance tests. The new modulus-return frequencies extend descriptive results without introducing uncertainty estimation.

E6.justification: Table 6 adds substantial resource and detection-error results, including TOPLOC's reported 0.26 ms/token commitment overhead and 81 ms validation time. Tables 3–4 newly report prompt/model error margins, and Table 11 adds modulus-return frequencies. Some plotted results are removed. Retained GPU, kernel and precision counts are equivalent match-to-mismatch conversions, not performance improvements.

T1.justification: Appendix C adds computational-complexity claims for interpolation, modular inversion, polynomial evaluation and modulus search, plus a uniform-input assumption supporting an exponentially decreasing search tail. This is a limited theoretical expansion; the central polynomial construction is retained and no security proof is added.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction and conclusion replace the quantified 'up to 100×' validation-speed claim with 'significantly faster.' The introduction also drops the claim of being first to empirically analyze transformer rounding errors. The principal compression, robustness and perfect observed detection claims remain.

C2.justification: New Sections 6.4–6.5 substantially expand the applicability discussion to activation spoofing and the difficulty of detecting subtle prompt edits or small fine-tuning updates. Section 5.4 adds a KV-cache error-accumulation explanation. Section 5.7 also explicitly explains the asymmetric precision acceptance already visible in v1's results.

D1.justification: Appendix C supplies detailed pseudocode for Newton interpolation, extended-Euclidean inversion, Horner evaluation and bounded modulus search. v2 also supplies TOPLOC repository and C++ implementation pointers absent from v1. These substantially expand reproducibility information, although the corresponding model-comparison table loses v1's explicit 2,000-prompt and 2,048-generated-token description.

R1.justification: v2 adds the bfloat16 and fp8 references by Kalamkar et al. and Micikevicius et al., removes the first-rounding-analysis novelty claim, and expands comparative positioning against existing verification methods. The main related-work categories and cited verification approaches remain.

P1.justification: The introduction and background are extensively condensed, repetitive experimental explanations are rewritten, contributions become a bullet list, and 'commits' largely becomes 'proofs.' The standalone contents page disappears, while the narrative gains an efficiency-comparison section and expanded limitations and appendices.

P2.justification: The single-column report becomes a two-column conference article. v1's service-workflow diagram and exponent-error plot disappear, the mantissa figure contracts from six panels to three, and several success-rate tables are replaced or consolidated into error-statistic displays. New comparison and modulus-distribution tables further change the presentation.

improvement.justification: v2 improves reproducibility through subroutine specifications and code pointers, and better qualifies its claims through expanded attack limitations and removal of the quantified 100× speedup claim. Error margins also make detection results easier to assess. These gains are moderated by removal of worst-case plots, incomplete benchmarking details for Table 6, and Table 5's caption incorrectly applying bf16 thresholds to fp32 results. The evidence supports a limited overall improvement.
